precepts.text: Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
precepts.point: Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac; faith wrought with his works and by works was faith made perfect, and he was called the friend of God. By works a man is justified and not by faith only, as Romans 2:13 said, and Rahab was justified by works when she sent the spies out another way. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
“Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?” Abraham was justified by his works because his works proved his faith. Offering Isaac was his action. “Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?” His faith was perfected by his works; he was proven faithful by them.

“And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness.” That is the scripture Paul quotes in Romans 4: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” The same belief Paul speaks of is the belief James says was fulfilled when Abraham laid his son on the altar. His belief was counted for righteousness, and his works showed that belief to be real, “and he was called the Friend of God.”

So Paul and James do not disagree. “Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only”, which goes back to Romans 2:13, that the doers of the law shall be justified. Abraham believed, and kept the commandments of God, and both went together.

precepts.text: The showbread, the continual meat offering, the continual burnt offering of the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the set feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings, to make an atonement for Israel, and all the work of the house of our God. Atone, justify, and reconcile are the same word, and the works are temple sacrifice. Brothers who do not study Paul speak evil of dignities, of Paul, Mark, and Luke, and the Lord blinds their minds until they teach that nations can be saved and end up back at Cesare Borgia. House negroes are the worst kind.
precepts.point: To him that worketh not, that offers no sacrifice, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness, as David describeth the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works. The Lord deemed Abraham faithful before he sacrificed animals.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Romans 4:2 says “For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.” What works is Paul talking about? Nehemiah condenses them into one verse: “For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.”

Continual means it was done all the time, daily, annually. And “to make an atonement” goes back to the word justify: atone, justify and reconcile are the same thing. So the works Paul is talking about are temple sacrifice, temple law. When Paul wrote, the temple was still standing and the Jews in Rome were still going to it and still sacrificing, and they believed their works were enough.

Abraham shows the order. In Genesis 15 the Lord promised the old man an heir out of his own bowels and seed as the stars, “And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” He was promised the land and he believed. Only then was he told to take the heifer, the goat, the ram and the birds and divide them. Faith came first, then the works.

When brothers don't study Paul's letters, they start saying Paul's letters are not authoritative, and speak evil of dignities, of Paul, Mark and Luke, because they weren't of the twelve. When you speak evil of dignities, your mind is blinded and you end up teaching a whole different gospel: that the nations can be saved. House negroes are the worst kind of negro. But this is the college course of this school. Know what the works are from Nehemiah, and nobody can come to your school or camp and confound you at Romans 4.

precepts.text: He that despised Moses' law died without mercy under two or three witnesses. Under Moses there was no grace: sins like breaking the Sabbath, homosexuality, and idolatry had no animal, and refusing to sacrifice at all meant death. You were indebted to continual offerings.
precepts.point: To him that worketh not, that offers no sacrifice, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness, as David describeth the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works. The Lord deemed Abraham faithful before he sacrificed animals.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Romans 4:4 says “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.” To him that offers sacrifices, the reward is not reckoned of grace or mercy, but of debt, because under Moses there was no grace. Hebrews shows it: “He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy under two or three witnesses”. Without mercy means without grace.

If you chose to do something worthy of death that an animal could not atone for, you had to die. If you broke the Sabbath, you couldn't atone with an animal. Homosexuality, you couldn't atone with an animal. Idolatry, you couldn't atone with an animal. And if you chose not to sacrifice at all, you had to die. So you were indebted to offer continual sacrifices all the time: continual burnt offerings, drink offerings, sin offerings.

The prophets said the temple would be destroyed. Once the temple is gone, where are your works? If your salvation rests on sacrificing an animal and there is no animal, no priest and no temple to atone with, by default you have condemned yourself. That is why faith in Christ has to supersede the works.

“But to him that worketh not”, him that does not offer sacrifice, “but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” Christ justifies the ungodly through his death. Just as with Abraham, who was counted faithful before he sacrificed animals, God “imputeth righteousness without works”. Israel could keep sacrificing while the temple stood, but Christ had to come first in their minds, or they were in debt.

precepts.text: Surely he hath borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; he was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities, the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep, the house of Israel, have gone astray, and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of my people; not all people, not the good nations, my people, and Isaiah was an Israelite. Show me where the Old Testament changed that and Christ died a second time for heathens. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities; he bare the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors, an intercessor who dies in your place. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for other nations.
precepts.point: It was not written for his sake alone, but for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Israel was accustomed to sacrificing; Paul says fine, but acknowledge Christ first, because if you put your faith in the animal and the temple falls, you have condemned yourself by default with no animal, no priest, and no temple.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Paul says Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” Our offences: whose? Isaiah 53 shows who Christ was delivered for. “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows”: this is Isaiah speaking of his people. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Maybe you are thinking that is everybody. Keep reading.

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Like sheep of the house of Israel. The us is the sheep. “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth”; he did not say one word. Then: “for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” Not all people, not all nations, not the good nations, not the not-so-bad ones. My people. And Isaiah was an Israelite. Now you know who the our is, who the all is, who the we is.

All the apologists online have to do is show us in the Old Testament where this changed and Christ came back a second time and died for heathens. Show where Isaiah says, oh yeah, I almost forgot the other nations. Peter said the unlearned and unstable wrest Paul’s letters as they do the other scriptures, but this is what Paul got it from.

“By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.” Many who? Israelites; the thought has not changed. “He bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” An intercessor is a mediator, someone who steps in and dies in your place. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for the other nations. Abraham believed without the works of sacrifice, and so must we: faith in the one delivered for our offences.

precepts.text: Seventy weeks, 490 years, are determined upon thy people and thy holy city, to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, atonement and justification, to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to anoint the most Holy. From the commandment to rebuild Jerusalem under Persia unto the Messiah the Prince under Rome; after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself, for his people, and the people of the prince that shall come, Titus and Vespasian, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, with the end thereof a flood, 70 AD, and desolations determined as Israel is scattered.

Israel was accustomed to sacrificing; Paul says fine, but acknowledge Christ first, because if you put your faith in the animal and the temple falls, you have condemned yourself by default with no animal, no priest, and no temple.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Christ was delivered for our offences. Daniel shows the same thing on the prophetic clock: “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”. Seventy weeks, 490 years, upon thy people: Daniel’s people, Israel.

For what? “To finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.” That is what Christ did when he died. Reconciliation goes back to the word atonement, and back to the word justification.

“From the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem”: the rebuilding under Persia. “Unto the Messiah the Prince”: Rome. “And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”. He would be killed, but not for himself. Who was he killed for? His people. That is what Isaiah said, and that is why Daniel says not for himself.

“And the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”: Titus and Vespasian. “And the end thereof shall be with a flood”: war, 70 AD. “And unto the end of the war desolations are determined”: Israel removed out of the land and scattered among all nations into slavery. When the temple was destroyed there was no priest and no temple left to atone with, so the one who put his faith in the animal instead of Christ condemned himself by default. Faith in Christ had to come first.

precepts.text: In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory. Not all the seed of Israel and anybody else, not the good nations, not the individual heathens with black friends. My righteous servant justifies many by dying on the cross for all twelve tribes.
precepts.point: It was not written for his sake alone, but for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Israel was accustomed to sacrificing; Paul says fine, but acknowledge Christ first, because if you put your faith in the animal and the temple falls, you have condemned yourself by default with no animal, no priest, and no temple.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Isaiah 53 says “by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many”. Somebody says, see, many means anybody. Isaiah has something for that: “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.”

Not all the seed of Israel and anybody else outside of Israel. Not all the good nations. Not individual heathens who say they have black friends. All the seed of Israel, all twelve tribes, shall be justified.

How? My righteous servant justifies many by dying on the cross, by laying on himself the iniquity of them all. That is the “justification” Paul speaks of when he says Christ “was raised again for our justification”, and it is why Romans 5 opens, “Therefore being justified by faith”. Who, according to the Old Testament, would be justified? Israel.

So when you read justification all throughout Paul’s letters, there should be no confusion about what he is talking about or who he is talking about. Abraham’s faith was imputed to him for righteousness, and “it was not written for his sake alone”, but for his seed who believe on him that raised up Jesus from the dead.

precepts.text: Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness; his faith was shown in his works.
precepts.point: Righteousness is immortal, and righteousness is defined by the law: it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments. Abram's faith showed itself in his works.

note.label: Genesis 15: The Covenant and the Four Hundred Years

precepts.why:
Paul asks what Abraham our father found “as pertaining to the flesh”, and answers from this very verse: “For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.”

“If Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.” Abraham had no cause to boast in the flesh. He believed the Lord who told him to tell the stars, “So shall thy seed be”, and that belief was counted for righteousness.

And righteousness is defined by the commandments, so his faith was shown in his works. Faith and obedience were never two separate things in Abraham: he believed God, and his belief was seen in what he did.

precepts.text: Circumcision was a seal of the righteousness of the faith Abraham had yet being uncircumcised.
precepts.point: It still has to be done. A covenant is a contract with terms; the covenant was confirmed to Jacob for a law, and circumcision is one of the laws within the covenant.

note.label: Genesis 17: The Covenant Sealed in the Flesh

precepts.why:
Circumcision is “a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.” Paul explains what it sealed: Abraham “received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised.”

He believed and obeyed first, and then circumcision sealed it. That is the order. Likewise a brother can come into the truth, get built up in the faith, and then go through with the process. But it still has to be done: the token of the covenant is in the flesh, and “the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken my covenant.”

precepts.text: Abraham considered not his own body now dead nor the deadness of Sarah's womb; he staggered not at the promise through unbelief.
precepts.point: Is any thing too hard for the Lord? The barren woman is made a joyful mother of children. Through faith Sarah received strength to conceive when she was past age, and Abraham, as good as dead at a hundred, staggered not at the promise but was strong in faith, fully persuaded that what He had promised He was able to perform.

note.label: Genesis 18: The Promise of Isaac and the Cry of Sodom

precepts.why:
Abraham “considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb.” He was as good as dead, and it had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women, yet “He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God”.

He was “fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.” That is the answer to “Is any thing too hard for the Lord?” Sarah laughed within herself; Abraham was fully persuaded. And at the time appointed the Lord returned according to the time of life, and Sarah had a son.

precepts.text: Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while yet uncircumcised.
precepts.point: To understand circumcision and uncircumcision you have to go to the origin: circumcision was the token, the sign, the seal of the covenant the Most High made with Abraham, a visible confirmation carried through all the generations.

note.label: Acts 11: The Gentiles Are Scattered Israel

precepts.why:
“And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised.”

Circumcision is the sign and the seal. Abraham had the faith first, while he was yet uncircumcised, and circumcision sealed the righteousness of that faith. It is the seal of the covenant, confirmed on his seed through all the generations.
